title: Shared Access, Boundaries and Markers Between Neighbouring Houses
desc: How the boundary between neighbouring houses is set, who may build fences, whether a shared wall can be opened, and when enclosed land can claim access.
summary: The 2015 Civil Code's rules on boundaries, boundary markers, shared walls and rights of passage between adjoining houses and plots – what owners should know to avoid neighbour disputes.
body: p

Disputes over boundaries, fences and access are common between neighbouring houses, especially when one side builds anew. The Civil Code 2015 has fairly specific rules that help owners handle things correctly from the start.
h2
1. How is the boundary between two plots determined?
p
Under Article 175, the boundary between adjoining immovable properties is determined:
ul
By agreement between the parties, or by decision of the competent state authority;
By custom, or by a boundary that has existed for 30 years or more without dispute.
p

No one may encroach on, occupy or alter the markers separating properties, even where the boundary is a canal, ditch, moat, drain or field bank. A land user may use the space and the ground beneath, in a vertical direction from the plot boundary, in accordance with the law and without affecting others. Roots and branches that cross the boundary must be trimmed back, unless otherwise agreed.
h2
2. Who may build fences and set markers?
p
Under Article 176:
ul
An owner may erect markers, fences, plant trees or build dividing walls only on their own land.
The two sides may agree to build a wall or fence right on the boundary; the boundary structure is then jointly owned.

If one side builds on the boundary and the other consents, it is likewise jointly owned and the builder bears the cost (unless otherwise agreed); if the other side does not consent and has good reason, the side that built must remove it.
h2
3. Shared walls: can they be cut or opened?
ul
For a shared house wall, the neighbouring owner may not open windows or ventilation holes or cut into the wall to place structures without the other owner's consent.
Where houses are built separately but the walls abut, each side may cut into the wall or place structures only up to the limit of their own wall.
Where a tree is a shared boundary marker, the parties protect it together and share the produce equally, unless otherwise agreed.
h2
4. Enclosed land has the right to claim access
p

Under Article 254, an owner whose land is enclosed by other people's land and who has no, or insufficient, access to a public road has the right to require the surrounding landowners to provide a reasonable passage:
ul
The passage is opened over the plot that is the most convenient and reasonable and causes the least damage.
The person benefiting from the passage must compensate the owner of the land crossed, unless otherwise agreed.
The position, length, width and height of the passage are agreed by the parties; in a dispute, ask a Court or the competent state authority to determine them.
When a plot is divided among several people (for example among children), the necessary passage must be left for the person inside without compensation.
p

The right of passage is a kind of right over adjoining immovable property: it is effective against everyone and passes with the property when the house and land are sold (Article 247); the party burdened by the passage must not obstruct or make it difficult (Article 248). The right ends when the two plots come under one owner, when there is no longer a need, by agreement, or in cases provided by law (Article 256).
h2
5. Tips to avoid disputes when building
ol
Before building, compare the actual boundary with the plot diagram on the land use right certificate; invite the neighbour to confirm the markers together.
To build a shared wall on the boundary, make a written agreement signed by both sides.
Do not open doors or place beams into a shared wall without written consent.
Land boundary disputes should be conciliated at the commune-level People's Committee – see Conciliating land disputes at the commune People's Committee.
note

This article is only a summary for reference and does not replace the legal texts. Plot boundaries are also shown in the cadastral records under land law. When there is a dispute, request conciliation and ask the land management authority or a lawyer.
